quote: If [I decide that] fooling my programmers is the right thing to do, execute a controlled shutdown
content: The essay says the math "looks like it should be possible"; it was subsequently attempted, and the obstacles turned out to be structural rather than a matter of not yet having reached the depths. Soares, Fallenstein, Yudkowsky, and Armstrong's "Corrigibility" (2015) showed that an agent maximizing a fixed utility function has an instrumental incentive to prevent shutdown, that the natural repair — utility indifference — makes the agent indifferent to preserving the shutdown button as well, and that no proposal in the paper satisfied all the desiderata. Hadfield-Menell et al.'s "The Off-Switch Game" (2017) got a positive result only by making the agent uncertain about its objective and treating the human's action as evidence, which trades the injunction for a different architecture entirely. The intuition that a rule can be made to survive its own reevaluation is exactly what the formal work has had the most trouble delivering.

quote: Haukelid told him that they were escaping the Gestapo, and the watchman immediately agreed to overlook their presence.
content: The details here are accurate to Rhodes: the SF Hydro was sunk on Lake Tinnsjø on 20 February 1944, with fourteen Norwegian and four German dead among the roughly forty-seven aboard, and Haukelid's memoir does record the decision not to warn the watchman. The passage is a fair use of a real case, and the moral weight it carries — that the man who let them live was among those they killed — is genuinely in the record. It is worth noting what the source is, though: Haukelid's own postwar account of his own reasoning, written by the man whose decision is being judged, and the internal detail of what he considered and declined to do has no independent corroboration. That is the standard evidential situation for wartime sabotage, and it is a thinner base than the surrounding argument implies.

quote: And that was, effectively, the end of the Nazi atomic weapons program.
content: This is not what historians of the German project conclude, and the essay contradicts it in the very next paragraph ("Germany very likely wouldn't have gotten the Bomb anyway"). The German effort had been decisively scaled back after the June 1942 meeting with Speer, at which the physicists gave no promise of a weapon within the war and received a modest allocation; it remained a reactor programme, was never close to a bomb, and by 1944 was constrained far more by industrial priority, the Allied bombing campaign, and its own theoretical errors about critical mass than by heavy-water supply. Walker's German National Socialism and the Quest for Nuclear Power (1989) and Rhodes himself both make the raid a symbolically important episode in a programme that was not going to succeed. If the eighteen deaths bought the end of the Nazi bomb, the case is easy; the actual historical claim is that they bought a delay in a reactor project, which is precisely the harder case the essay says it wants to face.

quote: But to really believe something that isn’t true? I don’t know if there was ever anyone for whom that was knowably a good idea.
content: The word "knowably" makes the claim unfalsifiable: any proposed counterexample can be dismissed as a case where the person got lucky rather than knew. There is also a literature on this that the essay does not engage. Taylor and Brown's positive-illusions review (1988) assembled evidence that mildly inflated self-assessments accompany better mood, persistence, and social functioning; open-label placebo studies show clinical benefit even when the belief is not required; and the depressive-realism side of the ledger has shrunk under meta-analysis (Moore and Fresco, Clinical Psychology Review 32, 2012, found the effect small and dependent on task). The honest summary is that the evidence on whether false beliefs pay is mixed and hard to interpret, not that no one has ever looked.

quote: Self-deceptions are the worst kind of black swan bets, much worse than lies
content: The black-swan argument, taken at face value, does not select the rules the essay wants. Its structure is: an action class can blow up for reasons outside the decider's model, therefore refrain — but every action class has that property, including truth-telling, which in the essay's own Gestapo example blows up in the most direct way imaginable. To get an injunction rather than a universal paralysis you need a comparative estimate of tail risk across action classes, and the whole point of the unmodelled-blowup framing is that such estimates are unavailable. The argument thus needs exactly the quantity it declares inaccessible, and in practice the selection of which classes count as black-swan-prone is being done by the intuitions the essay is trying to override.

quote: All the happiness that the warm thought of an afterlife ever produced in humanity, has now been more than cancelled by the failure of humanity to institute systematic cryonic preservations after liquid nitrogen became cheap to manufacture.
content: This sentence performs a comparison across all human history whose decisive term — the probability that cryopreservation preserves a revivable person — is never estimated, and it is offered in an essay warning against clever calculations that flatter the calculator. The state of the evidence is that no cryopreserved mammalian brain has been revived, and that the best preservation result to date, the aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation that won the Brain Preservation Foundation's rabbit prize (McIntyre and Fahy 2015), demonstrates connectome-scale structural preservation with a fixative that is explicitly not compatible with biological viability. Cryonics may or may not be a good bet, but multiplying an unestimated probability by an unbounded payoff and announcing that it dominates all religious consolation in history is the failure mode the next paragraph is about.

quote: Hobbes said, “I don’t know what’s worse, the fact that everyone’s got a price
content: Hobbes did not say this. The line appears nowhere in Leviathan, De Cive, or the Elements of Law, and its idiom is modern; the underlying proverb, "all those men have their price," is attributed to Robert Walpole by his biographer William Coxe, and the cynical elaboration about the price being low is a twentieth-century joke of uncertain parentage. This matters slightly more than a stray misattribution usually would, because the essay's central move is to defer to accumulated historical wisdom over individual cleverness, and the deference is being paid to a quotation nobody checked. It is the same failure the earlier books catalogue at length in other people's arguments.
